summary:
FieldRota is a free web tool that helps a farmer choose the next three years of crops for their own fields: a crop rotation, meaning different crops grown on the same field in turn (for example wheat, then chickpea, then sunflower). The farmer finds their fields on a satellite map, says what they grow now and picks a priority: save water, build soil, or balance both. FieldRota then suggests a rotation and shows the well water it saves, average income, nitrogen left in the soil, the local crop rules and a sowing calendar, and checks the plan against the 2050s climate with six climate models.
We built it first for the Konya Plain in Türkiye, where NASA’s GRACE satellites show groundwater falling by about 3.4 cm a year and new crop rules start in 2027. There, the suggested rotation (barley, vetch, canola) needs 48% less well water than today’s maize, wheat and sugar beet, and all six models agree it still saves water in the 2050s. The same method works anywhere: we tested it in Kansas, Punjab, California and La Mancha, where it cuts well water by 29–87%. It matters because it turns NASA data into one clear decision a farmer can act on this season.
details:
The problem. The Konya Plain is Türkiye’s breadbasket, and it is running out of groundwater. NASA’s GRACE satellites show the groundwater over the basin falling by about 3.4 cm a year. AFAD has mapped 739 sinkholes on the plain, and about three in four of the basin’s roughly 160,000 wells are unlicensed. Summers are also getting hotter: Çumra had about 4 days over 35 °C a year in 1985–1994, 14 a year in 2015–2025 and 35 in 2025 alone. From 2027, irrigated fields in Çumra must follow a new crop list and rotation rules. Every farmer there asks the same question: what should I plant next?

What FieldRota does. FieldRota answers that question for one farmer’s own fields, in four steps:

  1. Mark your fields. Spin a 3D globe of NASA Blue Marble imagery, pick your country and province, and zoom in to the satellite image. Click inside each field: FieldRota finds the field’s edge on the image and measures its area. You can add as many fields as you farm, or draw the corners yourself.
  2. Say what you grow. Enter your current three-year rotation and farm size.
  3. Choose what matters. Save water, build soil, or balance both.
  4. Get your rotation. FieldRota scores every possible three-year rotation and shows the best one with: the well water it saves, average income, soil health and the nitrogen legumes leave behind (as bags of urea saved), a check against the 2027 rules, the soil near your fields and a month-by-month sowing calendar. One switch replays the same plan in the 2050s climate.

How it works. Daily NASA POWER weather (1985–2025) drives the climate checks for each crop: heat at flowering, frost after sowing and how well temperatures fit the crop. In Konya, crop water use comes from field measurements at Çumra (TAGEM–DSİ 2017) and POWER rainfall is scaled to the local weather station. Everywhere else, water demand is computed with the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith method from NASA POWER. For the 2050s, we take the monthly change from six NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 climate models (2041–2060 vs 1995–2014) and add it to the observed weather. Field outlines come from NASA HLS (30 m) and ESA Sentinel-2 (10 m) images, analysed in the browser. Soil texture, organic carbon and pH come from ISRIC SoilGrids. Local rules, prices and support payments plug in per country; for Konya they are loaded.

What we found. On a typical Çumra farm, today’s grain maize, wheat and sugar beet rotation will not be allowed from 2027. With water as the priority, FieldRota suggests barley, vetch and canola: 242 m³ less well water per decare every year (48% less), soil health up from 32 to 86 out of 100, and all six climate models agree it still saves water in the 2050s. We show the trade-off openly: average income is lower than today’s rotation (about ₺850,000 vs ₺1.8 million a year on 100 decares, before seed, fertiliser and diesel), so the farmer can weigh water against money. There is also a middle path: wheat, canola and dry bean is allowed in 2027, uses 33% less well water, keeps about 89% of today’s average income (₺1.61 million vs ₺1.80 million on 100 decares) and raises soil health to 82; all six models agree it still saves water in the 2050s. We tested the same method in four other groundwater hot spots seen by GRACE: Kansas (29% less well water), Punjab (74%), California’s Central Valley (87%) and La Mancha in Spain (65%).

Why it matters. Most climate and satellite tools stop at maps and averages. FieldRota ends with one plan a farmer can act on this season, for their own fields, with every number and its source on the page. Saving water at field scale, across thousands of farms, is how a basin stops losing its aquifer.

What is new. Field edges are found from the satellite image right in the browser, so a farmer does not need maps or GPS files. The plan is tested against six climate models, not one. The tool says plainly what it does not know: global crop calendars are approximate, and income does not include all costs. It runs as a single static page with no server, so it is free to host and works on a phone.

Tools. Python (pandas, NumPy, rasterio) for the data pipeline; JavaScript with d3 and TopoJSON for the map and charts; HTML and CSS for the page.

Use of AI. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant to brainstorm, research, write and debug code, analyse data, draft and translate texts, and design the slides and page layout. Every AI-assisted code file says so in its header, and the README explains it. No images were AI-generated: satellite imagery is NASA Blue Marble, NASA HLS and Sentinel-2, and screenshots are from our own app. We checked the numbers and sources ourselves.

Limits and next steps. We have not yet tested FieldRota with farmers on their real fields; that is our first next step, in Çumra. Field edge detection works best inside the sharper 10 m image areas. Soil comes from SoilGrids sample points, so a lab soil test is still more exact. Next, we want to draw fields straight from land registry parcel numbers, run a small server so any farm on Earth can be analysed live, and add local rule and price plug-ins for more countries.
